grows.d: The strength to try again when it's hard
lv: Tends to give up quickly when things get hard.
This is natural at this age. Praise the act of trying again rather than the result, and start with easy steps your child can succeed at. "Shall we try just once more?" works better than "Finish it."
Sticks with things they love, but needs help with hard ones.
Break tasks into small steps so your child experiences "just one more." Taking a break and coming back is persistence too.
Has solid strength to try again and see things through, even when it's hard.
Deep focus can make stopping midway hard. So they don't wear themselves out chasing perfection, let them know "This is good enough."

grows.d: The strength to decide and do things on their own
lv: Still needs a lot of help and decisions from adults.
Wait just 10 seconds before doing it for them. Things change as they build up experiences of finishing tiny tasks, like one sock, on their own.
Does familiar things alone, but looks for an adult with new things.
Start with small choices, like picking one of two. It's important that adults don't change what they chose.
Has solid strength to decide and do things on their own.
Widen their choices, but keep safety rules clear. When a strong "I'll do it!" leads to a tug-of-war, the easiest fix is simply allowing more time.

grows.d: The strength to read others' feelings and work together
lv: Their own wants still come first.
This is common at young ages. Put faces into words, like "Your friend looks sad," and practice short turn-taking through play.
Shares and waits well in a good mood, but finds it hard when they really want something.
Games where turns are visible, like taking turns stacking blocks or board games, work well. Notice the moment they waited, right away.
Has solid strength to read others' feelings and get along together.
So they don't lose sight of their own feelings by always giving in, also practice saying "No" and "I want a turn too."

E.sum: Moves first in front of new places, games and people. A child who learns by diving in with their whole body.
E.det: Children high in Explorer see new things as chances rather than threats. They learn by doing rather than listening to explanations, and they need plenty of time to use their bodies each day. Because they sometimes move before they look, safety rules work best when they are short, clear and set in advance.
E.st: Adapts quickly to new settings and enjoys challenges.
E.wa: Needs practice stopping to look before moving.
E.say: You want to try it first! Let's agree on just one rule and go.
says: Arriving at a new playground
You want to try it first! Let's agree on just one rule and go.
Trying to climb somewhere that looks risky
You wanted to climb up! Hold Mom's hand and let's go just this far.
Somewhere they have to wait quietly
Your body feels wiggly, right? Let's count to ten, then go out and run.
Suddenly walking up to a child they've never met
You want to play together! Let's ask first: "Want to play?"

I.sum: Watches carefully and moves once ready. Once comfortable, they dive in deeply.
I.det: Children high in Observer gather information first in new situations. This isn't shyness; it's their own safety check. Rushing makes them pull back, while waiting lets them step forward on their own. Arrive a little early at new places to give them time to look around, and don't force them to greet people they've just met.
I.st: Careful, makes few mistakes and focuses deeply on familiar things.
I.wa: Needs plenty of time to adjust to new settings.
I.say: It's okay to just watch first. Tell me when you want to try.
I.no: All the other kids are doing it, why won't you?
says: Going somewhere new for the first time
It's okay to just watch first. Tell me when you want to try.
When an adult tells them to say hello
Just waving is fine for now. You can say hi when you're ready.
Watching other kids play without joining in
You're watching how they play. Shall we go a little closer together?
Before starting a new activity
Today we're going to do this. Let's watch once first, then decide.

S.sum: Feels small differences in sound, touch and mood. That also means they tire easily.
S.det: Children high in Sensitive take in the same stimulation bigger and in more detail. Struggling with how clothes feel or with noisy places isn't stubbornness; it's real discomfort. After busy days, build in quiet rest time. As they grow, this sensitivity becomes the base for observation, empathy and an eye for beauty.
S.st: Observant and quick to notice how others feel.
S.wa: Tires quickly in busy places, so needs time to rest.
S.say: That felt uncomfortable, didn't it? Can you tell me what it feels like?
S.no: It's nothing, why are you making a fuss?
says: Saying clothes or socks feel uncomfortable
That felt uncomfortable, didn't it? Can you tell me what it feels like?
In noisy, crowded places
That was too loud, wasn't it? Let's rest somewhere quiet for a bit.
Getting very startled or crying over small things
That really surprised you. Let Mom hug you. Let's breathe slowly.
Disliking a food's taste or smell
This taste is new to you. Just one bite, and you can leave the rest if you don't like it.

N.sum: Isn't shaken much by most stimulation or change. Gets right back up after a fall.
N.det: Children high in Easygoing have a high threshold for discomfort, so they do well almost anywhere. But they say little even when uncomfortable or hurt, so adults can easily miss it. They may also miss subtle changes in other people's faces, so putting feelings into words helps.
N.st: Stays steady when things change and recovers quickly from stress.
N.wa: Rarely voices discomfort, so adults need to ask first.
N.say: You look okay, but let me ask. How do your body and heart feel right now?
N.no: You never care about anything anyway.
says: Seeming fine after a fall
You look okay, but let me ask. How do your body and heart feel right now?
Staying quiet after a friend grabs their toy
Didn't that upset you just now? If you don't like it, you can say "That's mine."
Playing on without mentioning they're hurt
It's red here. If something hurts, always tell Mom, okay?
Not picking up on the mood around them
Shall we look at your little sibling's face? How do you think they feel?

F.sum: Shows joy and upset big and clearly. Wants to share what's in their heart.
F.det: Children high in Expressive have high emotional volume. Parents can read them easily, but reasoning doesn't work while feelings are running high. First name the feeling, then talk once things calm down. It helps to agree in advance on safe ways to let big feelings out, like stomping or hugging a pillow.
F.st: Doesn't hide feelings, so they're easy to read and full of affection.
F.wa: Needs time and a way to calm down in big emotional moments.
F.say: You're really, really upset. When you're done crying, let's talk together.
F.no: Stop crying. It's nothing to cry about.
says: Crying loudly or getting angry
You're really, really upset. When you're done crying, let's talk together.
Getting loud from excitement
You're so excited! Please use a small voice here.
About to throw something in anger
It's okay to be angry. Instead of throwing, let's stomp our feet.
When upset feelings last a long time
Some of that feeling is still there. Mom will stay right beside you.

T.sum: Doesn't show feelings in a big way and handles them inside. Returns to their usual self quickly.
T.det: Children high in Calm don't show their ups and downs much, so they're easily seen as simply easy babies. It's not that they don't feel; they just show less. Instead of "Are you okay?", ask specifically, like "How was that thing earlier?", and open up other ways to express feelings, such as drawing or play.
T.st: Calm and not swept away by feelings, bringing a sense of steadiness to others.
T.wa: Their inner feelings are easy to miss, so ask specific questions.
T.say: You don't have to say it. Could you show me with a drawing instead?
T.no: You're so easy, I never have to worry about you.
says: Looking upset but not saying anything
You don't have to say it. Could you show me with a drawing instead?
Only answering "I'm fine"
You said you're fine, but Mom is curious. Can you tell me a little?
Showing little reaction even to happy things
You smiled a little! I'm happy I can see you like it.
Trying to hold it in alone
You don't have to hold it in alone. If it's hard, squeeze Mom's hand.

J.sum: Feels at ease within set routines and order. Follows along well when told in advance.
J.det: Children high in Rhythm feel secure when they know what's coming next. Sudden changes shake them a lot, but a 5-minute warning and a daily schedule alone can prevent many conflicts. On days when routines break, like trips or events, at least keep sleep and mealtimes steady.
J.st: Builds good habits and keeps promises and rules well.
J.wa: Struggles with sudden changes, so tell them in advance.
J.say: When the long hand gets to 6, we'll tidy up. After that, it's bath time.
J.ph: and feels at ease with a predictable routine
says: Needing to end play and tidy up
When the long hand gets to 6, we'll tidy up. After that, it's bath time.
When plans suddenly change
The order changed today. Instead, I promise we'll go tomorrow.
Upset because it's not the usual way
You wanted to do it the usual way. Let's try it this way just this once.
Before going somewhere unfamiliar
Today we'll get in the car first, go to the doctor, and then come home.

P.sum: Moves with the flow of the moment. Keeps up easily even when plans change.
P.det: Children high in Free handle change well and sleep and play well anywhere. On the other hand, habits like sleeping and eating at set times don't form on their own. Rather than fixing every routine, lock in just one or two essentials, like the bedtime order, and give choices within them; they'll accept it well.
P.st: Flexible with change and enjoys new situations.
P.wa: Adults need to fix one or two essential routines.
P.say: Brushing teeth or reading a book, which do you want to do first?
P.no: Why do you always do whatever you want?
says: Putting off getting ready for bed
Brushing teeth or reading a book, which do you want to do first?
So into play they can't move on
It's fun, right? Let's stack just five more blocks, then go.
Toys scattered everywhere
Should the cars go in first, or the dolls? You decide.
Running late in the morning
Shoes on before this song ends. Ready, go!

items.t: Quickly wanders around and explores even in a place they've never been.
items.ex: At an indoor playground or a relative's home for the first time, leaves your side to look around alone

items.t: Prefers active play to sitting still.
items.ex: Even during story time, gets up to walk around or moves their body

items.t: Goes up to children they've just met to talk or play.
items.ex: At the playground, says "Let's play!" to a child they've never seen, or plays next to them

items.t: Is bothered by small textures like clothing tags or sock seams.
items.ex: Asks you to cut off tags or only wants to wear certain clothes

items.t: Notices quickly when things at home are moved.
items.ex: When furniture moves or something new appears, asks "What's this?" as soon as they come in

items.t: Gets upset or worried easily, even over small things.
items.ex: Cries when a drawing doesn't turn out right or a cracker breaks

items.t: Shows joy with the whole body, shouting or jumping up and down.
items.ex: Shouts "Wow!" and bounces around when getting a present

items.t: Talks about what happened or how they feel without being asked.
items.ex: On the way home from daycare, says "A friend pushed me today" without being asked

items.t: Takes a while to calm down once crying or angry.
items.ex: Crying goes on for over 10 minutes or takes a long time to soothe

items.t: Gets sleepy and hungry at about the same times every day.
items.ex: You can guess nap time and snack time without looking at a clock

items.t: Accepts ending play much better when warned in advance.
items.ex: Fusses less if you say "We're going home in 5 minutes"

items.t: Wants things in their usual spot or done in a set order.
items.ex: Always puts shoes in the same place and dislikes it when the bedtime order changes

items.t: Tries again several times even when something isn't working.
items.ex: Rebuilds a block tower after it falls

items.t: Wants to dress themselves or tidy up on their own.
items.ex: Says "I'll do it!" and tries to put on shoes alone

items.t: Goes over to comfort a friend or family member who is crying.
items.ex: Brings a tissue or toy to a crying sibling or friend

items.t: Touches a new toy or game before hearing how it works.
items.ex: Presses the buttons as soon as a new toy box is opened

items.t: Often runs or climbs, even indoors.
items.ex: Jumps off the sofa or climbs onto chairs and the table

items.t: Hides behind a parent or hesitates when an unfamiliar adult talks to them.
items.ex: Hides without answering when a neighbor in the elevator asks "How old are you?"

items.t: Is startled by or dislikes loud sounds and bright lights.
items.ex: Covers ears or cries at the vacuum, hand dryer or fireworks

items.t: Picks up right away when a parent's face or voice changes.
items.ex: Asks "Mom, are you mad?" when a parent is tired or upset

items.t: Gets right back up after falling or making a mistake.
items.ex: Falls while playing, brushes it off and keeps playing

items.t: When angry or upset, shows it so big that everyone around knows.
items.ex: Cries loudly or lies on the floor when they can't get what they want at the store

items.t: Doesn't mention upsetting things unless asked.
items.ex: You only find out about a fight with a friend from the teacher

items.t: Quickly shifts attention to something else even when upset.
items.ex: Stops crying soon when shown a favorite toy

items.t: Falls asleep at very different times from day to day.
items.ex: Some days asleep at 8, other days after 10

items.t: Goes along easily even when plans suddenly change.
items.ex: Comes along without fuss when you go to the store instead of the planned playground

items.t: Tries to correct you with "That's not right" when game rules or promises change.
items.ex: Says "No, you have to do it like this" when the reading order or game rules change

items.t: Tries to finish games or crafts they've started.
items.ex: Only gets up after finishing a puzzle or coloring

items.t: Says clearly what they want to do.
items.ex: Chooses: "I'll wear this one," "Not this, that"

items.t: Shares toys or snacks.
items.ex: Offers a cracker while eating: "Want one?"

items.t: Only joins a new activity after watching for a while.
items.ex: At a trial class, watches the other kids for a few minutes before joining in

items.t: Enjoys quiet play like books or puzzles for a long time.
items.ex: Sits drawing or doing puzzles for over 20 minutes

items.t: Gets more excited in places where many people gather.
items.ex: Livelier than usual at birthday parties or family gatherings

items.t: Notices even small differences in how food tastes or feels.
items.ex: Refuses to eat when the usual milk or side dish brand changes

items.t: Carries on with what they're doing even when it's noisy or chaotic.
items.ex: Keeps playing even with the TV on or a sibling crying

items.t: Remembers scary scenes or stories for a long time and brings them up again.
items.ex: Brings up a scary scene from days ago at bedtime

items.t: Doesn't show much on the outside, whether in a good or bad mood.
items.ex: Just smiles quietly even when getting a gift they love

items.t: Often asks to be hugged or for you to stay with them.
items.ex: Comes for hugs many times a day or says "Stay next to me"

items.t: Stays excited for a long time after something fun and is hard to settle.
items.ex: Too wound up to fall asleep until late after a day at an amusement park

items.t: Gets out of sorts when the usual routine changes.
items.ex: Fussier or crankier on days with a different routine, like trips or holidays

items.t: Wants to know the order in advance: "What are we doing next?"
items.ex: Asks in the morning, "Where are we going today? And after that?"

items.t: Switches games as ideas pop into their head.
items.ex: Suddenly switches from playing house to doctor to cars

items.t: Quickly says "I can't" and quits if something looks hard.
items.ex: If a button doesn't go in once, immediately says "Mom, do it for me"

items.t: Wants adults to do even small things for them.
items.ex: Asks for help with using a spoon or putting on socks even though they can do it

items.t: Finds waiting for a turn very hard.
items.ex: Pushes the child in front or cuts in line at the slide

items.t: Seeks new games more than familiar ones.
items.ex: Picks a toy they've never seen before their usual blocks

items.t: Seems to have energy left even after playing all day.
items.ex: Runs around at home again even after 2 hours at the playground

items.t: Takes time to feel comfortable with new friends.
items.ex: Only mentions friends' names a week or two into a new term

items.t: Doesn't mind much when clothes get wet or hands get dirty.
items.ex: Keeps playing in wet clothes after water play

items.t: Reacts to even small sounds or smells: "What's that?"
items.ex: Is the first to notice a distant siren or the smell of food

items.t: Holds on to being scolded or corrected for a long time.
items.ex: Brings up a morning scolding again in the evening, or stays glum

items.t: Laughs or cries loudly.
items.ex: Laughs or cries loud enough to be heard from another room

items.t: Shows things they made or did and waits for your reaction.
items.ex: Draws a picture and shows it again and again: "Look at this!"

items.t: Even when feelings rise, returns to their usual self in a moment.
items.ex: Angry one minute, playing as if nothing happened 1 to 2 minutes later

items.t: Eats very different amounts from day to day.
items.ex: Ate a whole bowl yesterday, only a few spoonfuls today

items.t: Finds it hard to stop in the middle of something and move on.
items.ex: Strongly objects when called to eat while building blocks

items.t: Likes sorting toys by type or lining them up.
items.ex: Lines up cars by color or groups blocks by shape

items.t: Focuses for a long time on activities they enjoy.
items.ex: Spends over 30 minutes on favorite blocks or drawing

items.t: Shows a "I can just try again" attitude after mistakes.
items.ex: Spills water and, instead of crying, tries to wipe it up or pours again

items.t: Tries to stop when told someone doesn't like what they're doing.
items.ex: Stops teasing when told "Your sibling says it hurts"

items.t: Returns to what they were doing even after being interrupted.
items.ex: Goes back to a craft after finishing a meal

items.t: Feels proud of things they managed on their own.
items.ex: Dresses alone and boasts, "I did it all by myself!"

items.t: Accepts a friend's ideas when playing together.
items.ex: Goes along with "This time let's play what you want"

items.t: Moves on to something else as soon as it gets a little boring.
items.ex: Pulls out another toy after less than 5 minutes on one game

items.t: Can't decide what to do on their own and hesitates a long time.
items.ex: Can't pick a snack for a long time, or says "Mom, you choose"

items.t: Quits a game when things don't go their way.
items.ex: Says "I'm not playing" and leaves after losing or not getting the role they want
